The Uncoupling of State and Altar: A Case for the Complete Privatization of Marriage

For centuries, the institution of marriage has existed at a powerful and often problematic intersection of the private heart and the public record. It has been simultaneously a sacred vow, a social ritual, a economic partnership, and a state-licensed status conferring a labyrinth of rights and obligations. It is this final aspect—the state’s role as gatekeeper and regulator of intimate unions—that has become an anachronistic, inequivalent, and ultimately unnecessary intrusion into the private lives of citizens. The time has come for a bold and liberating reform: not merely to expand who can access the institution, but to dismantle the institution’s legal scaffolding entirely. Marriage must be wholly removed from the sphere of government recognition and regulation, and redefined solely as a private relationship or contract between consenting adults.

The historical argument for state involvement in marriage is rooted in antiquated concerns of property transfer, lineage legitimacy, and social control. Governments institutionalized marriage to regulate inheritance, ensure clear lines of succession, and enforce patriarchal structures that managed female sexuality and labor. This model served the interests of the state and the propertied class, not the well-being of the individuals within the union. In the 21st century, clinging to this framework is indefensible. We no longer require the state to legitimize parentage for inheritance (paternity tests and birth certificates suffice), to manage property (contract and trust law exist), or to police intimate relationships. The state’s continued role as a marriage licensor is a vestigial organ of social control, applying a one-size-fits-all solution to the infinite variety of human bonds.

Furthermore, the state’s regulation of marriage is inherently discriminatory and a catalyst for perpetual conflict. Every expansion of marriage rights—interracial marriage, same-sex marriage—has been a decades-long battle against the state’s own discriminatory definition. This proves the fundamental flaw: by creating a privileged category, the state automatically creates outsiders. The fight for marriage equality, while just and necessary within the current system, ultimately reinforces the state’s authority to define and grant privilege to certain relationships over others. True equality is not achieved by inviting everyone to a party where the host sets the guest list; it is achieved by removing the host’s power to exclude. Abolishing state marriage eliminates the legal battlefield altogether, rendering discrimination by the state impossible because it no longer has a role to play.

The practical and legal entanglements created by state-sanctioned marriage are a quagmire of complexity and injustice. The system creates a binary: the married, who receive over 1,000 federal benefits and countless state-level ones, and the unmarried, who receive none. This penalizes the single, the polyamorous, those in long-term platonic partnerships, and caregiving relationships that do not fit the conjugal model. Why should a person visiting their partner in a hospital be denied access because they lack a state-issued marriage license? Why should cohabiting partners of decades have no automatic rights upon separation or death, while a newly married couple does? This arbitrary privilege distorts social and economic decisions, pressuring people into a legal contract for practical benefits rather than for the purity of the relationship itself.

Abolishing state marriage does not mean abolishing commitment, love, or ceremony. It means liberating them. Couples (or triads, or any consensual grouping) would be free to craft their own bespoke agreements—private marriage contracts, civil union agreements, or cohabitation covenants—drafted with lawyers to suit their unique needs. These contracts could specify property division, custody arrangements, healthcare directives, and inheritance, without the default, often ill-fitting template imposed by the state. Religious and cultural ceremonies would flourish, unshackled from legal significance, purely as expressions of personal and communal values. The state would simply recognize these private contracts under existing contract law, just as it recognizes business partnerships or real estate agreements.

Critics will argue that the state has a compelling interest in protecting vulnerable parties, especially children. This concern is valid but misplaced. Protections can be achieved without the monolithic institution of marriage. Modern family law can be reformed to focus on the best interests of children regardless of parents’ marital status, using the same tools of custody, child support, and guardianship that already apply to unmarried parents. Protections for domestic violence, financial abuse, and economic dependency can be enshrined in standalone laws that apply to all intimate relationships, not just marriages. In fact, decoupling legal protection from marriage would increase security for those in non-marital relationships who currently lack any automatic safeguards.

Ultimately, the state’s recognition of marriage is a paternalistic act that presumes its citizens cannot manage their most intimate affairs without a government blueprint. It is a system born of outdated social engineering that now serves primarily to create legal inequality and administrative complexity. By privatizing marriage, we affirm a profound respect for personal autonomy and pluralism. We allow relationships to be defined by love, commitment, and mutual agreement, not by a government checkbox. We replace a rigid, exclusive, and conflict-generating institution with a flexible, inclusive, and private framework. The state should get out of the marriage business altogether, leaving it where it belongs: in the realm of the heart, the home, and the private contract between free and equal citizens. Let marriage be a promise, not a permit.

In summary, the rationale for abolishing legal marriage is rooted in a philosophy that prioritizes absolute individual sovereignty and minimal government. It envisions a society where all relationships are voluntary, privately arranged, and free from state control, replacing a public status with private contract law. The Case for Ending State Marriage: Why Government Should Get Out of the Marriage Business

Introduction

For centuries, marriage has occupied an unusual and contradictory position in liberal democracies: it is simultaneously presented as a deeply personal, sacred, and private commitment—and yet it is one of the most heavily regulated, licensed, and state-defined relationships in existence. Governments decide who may marry, how marriages are formed, what obligations they create, and under what circumstances they may be dissolved. The state stamps its imprimatur on intimate relationships in a way it does virtually nowhere else in private life.

This essay argues that this arrangement is neither necessary nor desirable. Marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere of state recognition and treated solely as a private relationship, religious rite, or contractual arrangement between consenting adults. The government's role in licensing, defining, and regulating marriage should be completely abolished—not reformed, not expanded, but ended.

This position is not as radical as it may first appear. It is grounded in longstanding principles of individual liberty, limited government, religious freedom, and equal treatment under law. And far from creating chaos, removing state marriage would clarify legal obligations, expand genuine freedom, and resolve some of the most intractable political conflicts of our time.

I. Marriage Licensing Has a Deeply Troubling History

Any honest examination of state marriage must begin with an uncomfortable truth: government-issued marriage licenses were not originally created to celebrate love or protect families. They were created to control who could form families.

In the United States and many other nations, marriage licensing emerged as a tool of racial gatekeeping. Anti-miscegenation laws—which prohibited interracial marriage—required the state to approve or deny marriages based on the race of the applicants. These laws persisted in some American states until Loving v. Virginia in 1967, less than sixty years ago. The marriage license was, in its origins and for much of its history, a mechanism of exclusion, designed to preserve racial hierarchies by controlling the most intimate sphere of human life.

Beyond race, state marriage has historically been used to exclude same-sex couples, to prohibit marriages across religious lines, to restrict marriages by people with disabilities, and to impose waiting periods, residency requirements, and other bureaucratic hurdles that have nothing to do with the substance of a couple's commitment.

The history of state marriage is not a story of benevolent regulation. It is a story of the state claiming authority over intimate human relationships and using that authority to enforce social hierarchies. While many of the most egregious exclusions have been struck down by courts or repealed by legislatures, the underlying presumption—that the state has the rightful authority to define and license intimate relationships—remains unchallenged. It should be challenged.

II. The State Has No Legitimate Interest in Licensing Love

Defenders of state marriage often claim that the government has a legitimate interest in "promoting stable families" or "protecting children." These claims deserve scrutiny.

First, consider the logic of licensing. We require licenses for activities that pose genuine risks to public safety: driving, practicing medicine, carrying firearms, operating heavy machinery. Marriage, however, poses no comparable public safety risk. Two people deciding to commit to each other does not endanger third parties. The requirement that the state approve such a commitment before it becomes legally recognized is a historical artifact of paternalism and control, not a response to any genuine threat.

Second, the "family stability" argument proves too much. If the state's interest were truly in promoting stable families and child welfare, we would expect the legal framework of marriage to be carefully calibrated to those goals. It is not. Consider:

  • The state licenses marriages between people who have no intention of having children.
  • The state licenses marriages between elderly couples who cannot have children.
  • The state does not require any demonstration of parenting ability, emotional stability, or financial preparedness before issuing a marriage license.
  • The state does not revoke marriage licenses from couples who abuse or neglect their children.

If marriage licensing were truly about child welfare, the legal framework would look radically different. The fact that it doesn't reveals that the "child welfare" justification is largely post-hoc rationalization for a system that exists primarily because of tradition and inertia.

Third, the state's interest in child welfare can be fully served without marriage licensing. Child welfare laws, child support obligations, custody determinations, and protections against abuse can all exist independently of whether the parents are married. Many of these protections already do exist independently. Tying child welfare to the institution of marriage actually harms children by creating a two-tier system in which children of unmarried parents may receive less legal protection—when the children themselves had no say in their parents' marital status.

III. Private Contract Can Replace Every Legal Function of Marriage

One of the most common objections to abolishing state marriage is practical: "But what about all the legal rights and obligations that come with marriage—inheritance, hospital visitation, medical decision-making, tax benefits, immigration status?"

This objection assumes, incorrectly, that these rights and obligations can only be delivered through the institution of state marriage. In fact, every legal function of marriage can be replicated through existing or easily created private legal instruments:

  • Inheritance can be handled through wills, trusts, and beneficiary designations. These tools already exist and are widely used by unmarried couples, business partners, and others.

  • Hospital visitation and medical decision-making can be established through powers of attorney, healthcare proxies, and advance directives. These documents are inexpensive, widely available, and allow individuals to designate anyone they choose—not just a spouse—as their medical decision-maker.

  • Property division upon dissolution of a relationship can be governed by prenuptial or postnuptial agreements, cohabitation agreements, or general contract law. These tools allow couples to customize their arrangements to their actual circumstances rather than being subjected to one-size-fits-all state defaults.

  • Tax treatment should be neutral with respect to relationship status. The current system, which provides tax benefits to married couples, is a form of state subsidy for one particular relationship structure. There is no principled reason why a married couple should pay less tax than two unmarried people with identical incomes and identical expenses. Tax neutrality—or even the abolition of income tax in favor of other revenue mechanisms—would eliminate this distortion entirely.

  • Immigration status can be addressed through immigration policy reform that evaluates relationships on their own merits rather than relying on a binary married/unmarried distinction that invites fraud and creates perverse incentives.

The point is not that these issues are unimportant. The point is that they can all be addressed more precisely, more flexibly, and more justly through targeted legal instruments than through the blunt and historically exclusionary tool of state marriage.

Private contract also offers something state marriage does not: customization. Under the current system, when you get a state-licensed marriage, you are entering into a vast, complex, largely invisible bundle of legal rights and obligations that vary by jurisdiction and that you may not fully understand. A private contractual approach would require each couple to think deliberately about what they want their relationship to look like legally, rather than defaulting to a state-defined template that may not suit their circumstances.

IV. Abolishing State Marriage Resolves Irreconcilable Political Conflicts

Consider the political controversies that have surrounded marriage over the past several decades:

  • Same-sex marriage generated decades of bitter political conflict, constitutional litigation, and cultural warfare. In many countries, this conflict is still ongoing.

  • Polygamy and polyamory are increasingly discussed as the next frontier. If marriage is defined by consent and love, on what principled basis does the state exclude three or more consenting adults from a marital arrangement?

  • Interracial marriage, while now widely accepted, was illegal in parts of the United States within living memory.

  • Interfaith marriage remains controversial or legally restricted in many countries.

  • Divorce reform has been fought over for centuries, from the Catholic Church's historical prohibition to contemporary debates over no-fault divorce.

Every one of these conflicts arises because the state is in the business of defining and licensing marriage. When the state defines marriage, it must draw lines—and those lines will always exclude someone, generate controversy, and become a battleground for competing political and cultural visions.

Remove the state from the equation, and these conflicts evaporate—or at least, they cease to be political conflicts. If marriage is a private, religious, or contractual matter, then:

  • A same-sex couple can marry in a ceremony that reflects their values, with legal protections established through contract.
  • A conservative religious community can maintain its own definition of marriage without being compelled by the state to alter it.
  • A polyamorous group can establish contractual arrangements that reflect their relationship structure.
  • No one needs the government's permission to form the intimate relationships that are most meaningful to them.

This is not a utopian fantasy. It is a straightforward application of the principle that the government should not be in the business of defining or licensing intimate relationships. By removing state marriage, we remove the occasion for political conflict over the definition of marriage, and we replace it with a system of individual freedom and mutual respect.

V. State Marriage Undermines Religious Freedom

For religious communities, marriage is often understood as a sacred covenant, a sacrament, or a divine institution. The state's involvement in marriage creates a fundamental tension with this understanding.

When the state licenses marriage, it is claiming the authority to define a relationship that many people understand as properly defined by God, by religious tradition, or by the individuals themselves. This creates several problems:

  • Religious communities may feel compelled to perform or recognize marriages that conflict with their teachings, or they may fear that such compulsion is coming. (Whether or not this fear is legally justified, the political conflict it generates is real and damaging.)

  • Conversely, religious definitions of marriage may be privileged by the state in ways that disadvantage people whose beliefs or values differ. In many jurisdictions, religious leaders have special legal authority to solemnize marriages that civil officials do not, creating an inappropriate entanglement of religious and state authority.

  • The concept of "civil marriage"—marriage as defined by the state, distinct from religious marriage—is itself a relatively recent invention. Historically, marriage was primarily a religious or familial institution, and the state's involvement was limited. The modern system, in which the state claims primary authority over marriage and allows religious institutions a secondary role, inverts the historical relationship.

By abolishing state marriage, we restore marriage to its proper sphere: the private domain of individuals, families, and religious communities. A couple who wishes to marry can do so in a religious ceremony, a secular ceremony, a civil ceremony, or no ceremony at all—and their legal protections will be established by their own agreements, not by the state's definition.

This approach strengthens religious freedom by ensuring that no religious community is compelled to alter its definition of marriage, and no individual is forced to accept a religious community's definition. Each person and each community is free to define marriage according to their own values.

VI. The "Slippery Slope" Objection Fails

Critics might argue that abolishing state marriage would lead to chaos, exploitation, or the erosion of important social norms. This objection fails for several reasons.

First, social norms do not depend on state licensing. People did not stop valuing friendship because the state does not license friendships. People did not stop being good parents because parenting licenses do not exist. Marriage predates the modern state by thousands of years, and the social, cultural, and religious norms surrounding marriage are robust enough to survive the removal of a relatively recent bureaucratic overlay.

Second, exploitation can be addressed through general contract law and specific protective legislation without requiring state marriage. Laws against fraud, coercion, and abuse apply to all people in all relationships. Family law protections for children and vulnerable adults can exist independently of the institution of marriage.

Third, the current system already permits many of the harms critics fear. People enter exploitative marriages under the current system. People use marriage for immigration fraud under the current system. People enter marriages without understanding the legal consequences under the current system. Abolishing state marriage would not create these problems; it would merely change the legal framework within which they are addressed—and a contractual framework would likely be more transparent and more protective than the current opaque bundle of state-defined rights and obligations.

VII. A Vision of Genuine Freedom

The argument for abolishing state marriage is ultimately an argument for genuine freedom—the freedom to define your most intimate relationships on your own terms, without seeking the government's permission or accepting the government's definition.

This is not an argument against commitment. It is not an argument against love. It is not an argument against family. It is an argument against the proposition that the state should be in the business of licensing, defining, and regulating the most personal aspects of human life.

Imagine a world in which:

  • Couples form their commitments through religious ceremonies, secular rituals, private agreements, or simple declarations—according to their own values, not the state's template.
  • Legal protections are established through clear, customized contracts that each party understands and agrees to, rather than through an invisible bundle of state-imposed obligations.
  • No one needs the government's permission to form the relationships that matter most to them.
  • Political battles over the "definition of marriage" become obsolete, because marriage is no longer a political category.

Introduction

The State Has No Legitimate Role in Marriage

1. Marriage Is a Private, Not a Public, Matter

Marriage is, at its core, a personal and emotional bond between individuals. The state has no more business regulating love and commitment than it does regulating friendships, religious affiliations, or personal beliefs. Yet, by granting legal recognition to marriage, the government effectively declares that some relationships are more valid than others—a form of state-sanctioned discrimination.

One of the most glaring problems with state-recognized marriage is that it grants special legal and financial benefits to married couples while excluding others. These privileges include:

  • Tax benefits (e.g., joint filing, spousal deductions)
  • Inheritance rights (automatic inheritance without a will)
  • Medical decision-making authority (spouses can make healthcare choices for each other)
  • Immigration benefits (spouses of citizens can obtain residency more easily)

Why should a married couple receive tax breaks while a committed, long-term unmarried couple does not? Why should a spouse have automatic inheritance rights while a close friend or sibling does not? These distinctions are arbitrary and unfair.

By abolishing state-recognized marriage, we eliminate these unjust privileges and create a system where all relationships are treated equally under the law. Individuals would still be free to enter into private contracts that replicate many of these benefits (e.g., wills, power of attorney, joint property agreements), but the state would no longer play favorites.

Historically, marriage was a tool of patriarchal control, where women were treated as property and denied legal personhood. While modern marriage laws have evolved, remnants of this legacy remain. For example:

Marriage, long regarded as a cornerstone of social and familial structure, has evolved from a sacred religious or civil ritual into a state-sanctioned legal institution governed by laws, contracts, and bureaucratic oversight. 2. Marriage Regulation Unfairly Discriminates and Erodes Equality

State recognition of marriage has historically been a tool of social exclusion and systemic inequality. For centuries, marriage was denied based on race, religion, gender, and sexuality—just as it was used to enforce colonial, patriarchal, and heteronormative norms. By replacing state-sanctioned marriage with a neutral legal framework, we eliminate all distinctions based on identity, orientation, or relationship configuration. State-recognized marriage often inflates the significance of a ceremonial moment—a single "I do"—without requiring the depth of ongoing negotiation and accountability. Governments don’t issue certificates for friendship, prestexpolsian luxury (long-term platonic partnerships), or business alliances—nor should they for intimate unions. The state has neither the authority nor the moral standing to define or mandate the most intimate aspects of human life. Marriage, when subject to government decree, becomes a mechanism of control, a tool of exclusion, and a vestige of hierarchical social planning. By abolishing state-recognized marriage and replacing it with a framework of private, enforceable contracts—combined with universally accessible, rights-granting legal tools—we honor the diversity, complexity, and fluidity of human relationships.

Marriage has always been, and always should be, a private bond. It’s time to restore it to its rightful place: not in the halls of government, but in the hearts of free, consenting individuals. Let the state register rights. Let communities and individuals consecrate love. Let marriage finally be free.

Abolish State Marriage: Let Private Relationships Govern Private Life

Marriage is one of the most intimate and consequential relationships people form. Marriage Is a Private Relationship, Not a Public Qualification

State Marriage Turns Personal Relationships Into Government-Defined Statuses

Legal marriage does more than record a private commitment. It creates a comprehensive status with consequences across taxation, inheritance, property, medical decision-making, immigration, employment benefits, family law, and social welfare. These consequences can be substantial, but they are bundled together under a single label.

That bundle is both overinclusive and underinclusive. It may grant advantages to people whose relationship does not resemble the model assumed by the law, while excluding people whose relationships involve genuine dependence and responsibility but do not fit the required form. A long-term unmarried couple, a group of adults caring for an elderly relative, close friends who share medical and financial responsibilities, and extended family members raising children may all have needs that marriage law does not address effectively.

Marriage has often functioned as a gatekeeping device. Governments have used it to distinguish “legitimate” from “illegitimate” families, to restrict interracial and same-sex relationships, to enforce gender hierarchy, and to deny legal recognition to people whose lives did not conform to dominant social norms. For example, inheritance rights could be established through wills, default succession rules based on demonstrated dependency, or beneficiary designations. Health-care decision-making could be assigned through explicit medical directives or durable powers of attorney. Property rights could arise from title, contribution, and contract. Financial support could be governed by agreements and, where children are involved, by parental responsibility. Housing rights could be protected through tenancy and ownership law. None of these questions requires a general legal status called marriage.

This approach would not erase relationships; it would prevent the state from privileging one relationship form over all others. Equality would mean that people receive legal protection because they have rights, responsibilities, or legitimate interests—not because they possess a government-issued marital status.

Some defenders of state marriage argue that marriage is necessary because it supplies a convenient package of rights and obligations. Adults could use private contracts to establish arrangements concerning:

  • ownership and division of property;
  • financial contributions and shared expenses;
  • responsibility for debts;
  • inheritance and beneficiary rights;
  • housing and tenancy;
  • caregiving obligations;
  • business or household management;
  • dispute resolution;
  • support during illness or disability;
  • arrangements for ending the relationship.

Standardized legal forms could make such agreements affordable and accessible. Public institutions could provide clear information and default rules for people who do not create contracts. But those defaults would concern specific legal questions, not confer a sweeping marital identity.

A child should not receive greater protection because the adults responsible for that child possess a marriage certificate. Direct regulation of parental responsibility would be more rational and more protective than relying on marriage as a proxy.

State marriage invites unnecessary government involvement in private life. Marriage licenses require people to register intimate relationships with public authorities. Divorce proceedings can require intrusive disclosures about finances, sexuality, property, and personal conduct. Family law may impose obligations based on assumptions that do not reflect the parties’ actual arrangements.

People would still need courts to resolve contract breaches, property conflicts, fraud, abuse, child-support claims, and caregiving disputes. But the nature of those disputes would be clearer. The state would have less incentive to monitor who lives with whom, which relationships are considered genuine, and whether couples meet official standards of family formation. A religious institution may call two people married, but that designation would not automatically determine their tax status, property ownership, inheritance rights, or parental obligations. Those matters would be handled through contracts and generally applicable laws.

This separation would protect religious liberty rather than undermine it. No religious group would be required to perform a ceremony it rejects, and no religious definition would control people outside that community. The state would cease trying to create a universal definition of marriage, allowing many definitions to coexist privately.

Common Objections Do Not Justify Maintaining State Marriage

One objection is that marriage provides stability. But stability comes from commitment, trust, shared responsibility, and social support—not from a government label alone. If legal rules are needed to enforce financial or parental duties, those duties can be established directly.

Another objection is administrative complexity. It is true that replacing marriage with contracts and targeted legal rules would require reform. But administrative convenience cannot justify a system that distributes rights through an arbitrary status. The current system is already complex, particularly for blended families, unmarried partners, caregivers, and people with multiple dependents. A direct, modular system could ultimately be clearer.

Some argue that marriage promotes social welfare by encouraging long-term relationships. The state may reasonably support child welfare, caregiving, and economic security, but it should do so through policies aimed at those goals. Subsidizing marriage as a proxy for stability rewards some households while overlooking others that perform the same social functions.

Finally, critics may fear that abolition would weaken commitment. Yet commitment is most meaningful when it is chosen rather than required by law. Couples who wish to make lifelong promises could do so publicly, privately, religiously, or contractually. Removing state marriage would not make commitment impossible; it would make commitment more genuinely voluntary.

A More Limited and More Just Legal Order

The abolition of state marriage would not mean the abolition of family law. It would mean refocusing law on legitimate interests rather than maintaining an all-purpose marital category. The state could continue to prohibit domestic violence, enforce contracts, protect children, regulate adoption, determine parentage, administer inheritance, and resolve property disputes. It could also provide neutral default rules for people who fail to make private arrangements.

What would end is the presumption that all these matters should be organized through one privileged relationship status. The law would recognize people’s actions and responsibilities directly. It would protect individuals whether they are married, unmarried, coupled, single, related, or part of a chosen family.

This would be a more liberal system because it would ask less of the state and more of voluntary agreement. It would be a more equal system because legal protection would not depend on fitting a favored social model. It would be a more honest system because it would distinguish emotional commitment from financial obligation, parenthood from partnership, and caregiving from romance.

Marriage can remain meaningful without being a government institution. People should be free to marry in the eyes of their faith, culture, community, or conscience. But no one should need state recognition to make a commitment, form a household, care for another person, or build a family.

The state should protect rights, enforce responsibilities, and prevent harm. It should not certify intimacy. For those reasons, marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and returned to the private domain where it belongs.

Marriage laws in most countries dictate who can marry whom based on a set of criteria determined by the state, including gender, number of partners, age (often with inconsistent thresholds), consanguinity, and citizenship.   • medical decision-makers;
  • hospital visitors;
  • inheritance beneficiaries;
  • property co-owners;
  • tax household members where appropriate;
  • immigration sponsors under clear dependency or family criteria;
  • guardians for children;
  • emergency contacts;
  • end-of-life decision-makers;
  • financial agents;
  • caregiving partners;
  • beneficiaries for insurance and pensions.

These legal tools should be accessible without requiring people to enter a state-defined marital status. The law should ask: Who has the relevant responsibility? Who has consented to what arrangement? Who is dependent on whom? Who owns what? Who is caring for a child? It should not ask: Are these people married?

State marriage creates inequality by privileging one lifestyle

Government marriage does not merely recognize relationships; it rewards a specific form of relationship. In many legal systems, married couples receive advantages unavailable to unmarried people. These advantages may include tax benefits, inheritance defaults, health insurance access, immigration preferences, evidentiary privileges, and simplified property rights.

Such benefits are often defended as support for family stability. But this defense assumes that marriage is the central or superior form of family life. That assumption is outdated and exclusionary. Stable families take many forms. A child may be raised by unmarried parents, a single parent, grandparents, extended relatives, or guardians. Adults may build durable support networks without romantic or sexual partnership. Some people are single by choice. Others cannot marry because of economic barriers, immigration concerns, disability-benefit penalties, cultural constraints, or personal history.

There is no principled reason for the state to favor married people over unmarried people as a class. If the government wants to support children, it should support children directly. If it wants to support caregiving, it should support caregivers directly. If it wants to protect economic dependency, it should protect dependency directly. Marriage is a poor proxy for all of these goals.

State marriage also creates unnecessary conflict between civil law and religious belief. The state becomes the battlefield for arguments it does not need to adjudicate.

Civil legal arrangements should be handled through neutral contracts and status rules that do not use or define marriage. Of course, separation can create real legal issues. Shared property must be divided. Children must be cared for. Financial dependency must be addressed. But those issues would exist with or without marriage. The problem is that marriage bundles many issues together under a single status, often without clear prior agreement.

A contract-based system would be more honest. People could decide in advance what commitments they are making and what happens if the relationship ends. Default rules could exist for co-ownership, child support, and unjust enrichment, but they would not depend on marital status. Courts would enforce specific obligations rather than dissolve a symbolic state-certified union.

This would reduce the fiction that the state can manage the emotional reality of intimate life. The law should handle concrete disputes, not pretend to govern love.

Abolition promotes individual autonomy

State marriage is often defended as a choice: no one is forced to marry. But the choice is distorted when the state attaches major legal and financial consequences to marriage. People may marry not because they want the state involved in their relationship, but because marriage is the only convenient way to access health insurance, immigration status, tax treatment, inheritance rights, or medical authority.

That is not true freedom. It is coercive bundling. The state says: accept this legally defined status, with all its historical baggage and default rules, or lose access to protections that may be essential.

Abolition would unbundle these rights and let people choose the legal arrangements they actually want. Romantic commitment would no longer be used as a gateway to unrelated civil benefits. People could protect one another without conforming to the state’s preferred relationship model.

This is especially important for people whose lives do not fit conventional categories. Polyamorous families, platonic co-parents, asexual partnerships, elder-care households, disabled adults who risk losing benefits by marrying, and chosen families all expose the inadequacy of marriage as a legal category. A neutral system would be more flexible and humane.

The state can regulate harm without regulating marriage

Abolishing state marriage does not mean abolishing legal protection. The state should still regulate coercion, abuse, fraud, exploitation, neglect, and violence. It should enforce contracts, protect vulnerable parties, ensure child welfare, prevent forced relationships, and provide remedies for economic injustice.

The difference is that these protections should not depend on marriage. Domestic violence laws should protect victims whether or not they are married to their abusers. Property law should recognize contributions and ownership regardless of marital status. Support obligations should arise from parenthood, contract, dependency, or unjust enrichment—not merely from marriage. Immigration law should detect fraud and recognize genuine dependency without requiring marital status as the sole proof of family. Medical privacy rules should allow individuals to designate trusted persons.

The state’s proper role is to protect rights and enforce obligations, not to certify intimacy.

Marriage has too much historical baggage to be a neutral legal institution

Marriage law has historically been entangled with patriarchy, property control, religious authority, racial hierarchy, sexual regulation, and gender inequality. In many societies, marriage once treated women as legal dependents, restricted interracial unions, stigmatized children born outside marriage, criminalized same-sex intimacy, and enforced rigid gender roles. Reforms have made marriage more equal, but the institution still carries the legacy of state control over family life.

Abolition does not deny that many marriages are loving and equal. It simply recognizes that the state does not need to preserve an inherited legal category rooted in outdated social control. People who cherish marriage can continue to marry in every personal, spiritual, and communal sense. What would disappear is not love, commitment, ceremony, or family. What would disappear is government licensing of those things.

That distinction matters. Abolishing legal marriage is not abolishing marriage as a social or religious practice. It is abolishing the state’s monopoly over its legal meaning.

Practical reform is possible

Abolition may sound radical, but the transition could be practical and orderly. The government could phase out marriage licenses and replace them with a menu of civil agreements and default legal designations. Existing marriages could be converted into customizable civil contracts, with parties allowed to retain, revise, or dissolve specific legal obligations. Parentage, custody, and child support would be handled independently. Tax codes would be rewritten around households, dependents, and individual income rather than marital status. Inheritance defaults would be based on designated beneficiaries or actual dependency. Health-care decision-making would rely on registered directives. Immigration law would use broader family and sponsorship criteria.

This would require effort, but the current system is already complex and often unfair. Administrative convenience is not a sufficient reason to preserve a status that distorts equality and autonomy. Legal systems routinely modernize when old categories no longer serve justice.

Answering the strongest objection

The strongest objection is that marriage provides a simple, widely understood package of rights. Without it, people may fail to protect themselves. A surviving partner may be left without inheritance. A dependent partner may be abandoned. A hospital may deny access to a loved one. A caregiver may lack authority.

These are real concerns, but they are arguments against poor legal design, not arguments for state marriage. The solution is to make rights easier to assign and obligations easier to understand. These protections can be broader and fairer than marriage because they would apply to people who are currently excluded.

Marriage is simple only because it is overbroad. It bundles many unrelated legal consequences into one status. Simplicity purchased at the cost of unfairness is not good law. A modern legal system can do better.

State marriage should be abolished because it gives the government an unnecessary and unjust role in defining intimate life. It privileges one relationship form over others, entangles civil law with religious and cultural meaning, distributes rights through an arbitrary status, and forces diverse families into a single legal mold. The legitimate purposes now served by marriage law—protecting children, enforcing obligations, recognizing property rights, supporting caregivers, and allowing medical or financial decision-making—can be served more directly through neutral legal tools.

Marriage may remain a profound personal commitment, a sacred religious covenant, a cultural celebration, or a private promise. But it should not be a state-administered legal status. The law should protect people, not certify love. It should enforce consent-based obligations, not privilege one model of family. It should recognize care, dependency, parenthood, and contract wherever they exist.

Abolishing state recognition and regulation of marriage would not destroy marriage. It would liberate it from government control—and liberate the law from an outdated institution that no longer deserves its privileged place.

Individual autonomy and freedom At the core of the case for abolition is a basic liberal ideal: adults should be free to form, define, and dissolve intimate relationships without state imposition. When the state confers special legal meaning on a particular social form—“marriage”—it privileges one model of intimate life and shapes behavior by attaching rewards and penalties. Removing the state from the marriage business restores autonomy: individuals and couples could define their relationships and arrange their affairs through private agreements tailored to their needs, values, and cultures, free from a one-size-fits-all legal template.

Equality and dismantling embedded hierarchies State-recognized marriage has historically reinforced exclusionary and patriarchal patterns—defining who counts as a legitimate family, legitimizing gender-based economic dependency, and criminalizing or marginalizing other relationship structures. While many legal reforms have expanded access—most notably the extension of recognition to same-sex couples—state marriage remains a structural privilege that benefits some people more than others and perpetuates inequalities for those who fall outside its bounds (cohabitants, polyamorous groups, non-romantic caregivers, etc.). Abolishing state-sanctioned marriage levels the playing field. Rights and protections would be distributed according to clear, neutral legal principles—contract, property, and parental law—rather than by whether a couple fit a historical or religious template.

Separation of church and state and pluralism For many, marriage is first and foremost a religious or cultural sacrament. The entanglement of religious rites with civil sanction undermines both religious freedom and secular governance. When the state licenses marriages, it implicitly endorses particular conceptions of family and morality. Removing state recognition honors pluralism: religious communities and private organizations remain free to solemnize and bless unions according to their beliefs, but such ceremonies would carry spiritual and communal significance only—not automatic civil consequences. This shift prevents the state from privileging particular religious or cultural definitions of family and ensures neutrality toward moral diversity.

Contractual clarity and legal efficiency Private law already provides robust tools—contract, trusts, wills, powers of attorney, and property law—to accomplish practically every legal function currently bundled into marriage. Treating intimate partnerships as a matter of private contract encourages clarity and voluntariness. Parties could draft precisely the obligations and benefits they want: financial arrangements, caregiving responsibilities, powers of attorney, tenancy rights, and custodial agreements. Reducing state power, bureaucracy, and perverse incentives Marriage as a legal institution permits widespread administrative entanglement: marriage licenses, spousal benefits across tens of thousands of laws, tax filing status, family law proceedings, immigration sponsorship schemes, and more. Abolishing state marriage would simplify legal regimes and reduce bureaucratic overhead. It would also remove perverse incentives created by the current system: coercive or economically dependent marriages formed to secure immigration status, health benefits, or retirement payments; prolonged litigation aimed at preserving tax advantages; and social pressure to maintain a legally recognized union even when personal ties have dissolved. The Case for Privatizing Marriage: Removing the State from Personal Relationships

Introduction

Marriage has transformed dramatically throughout human history—from religious sacrament to economic arrangement to civil institution. Yet one constant remains: government involvement in defining, regulating, and privileging certain relationships over others. This state entanglement with marriage has become increasingly problematic in our diverse, pluralistic society. The time has come to fully separate marriage from the state, removing it entirely from the legal sphere and recognizing it solely as a private relationship or contract between consenting individuals. The Historical Evolution of State Marriage

Marriage as we understand it today—a government-licensed relationship conferring special legal status—is relatively recent. For most of human history, marriages were private or religious affairs, primarily concerned with property rights, family alliances, and social organization. The government's role in licensing and regulating marriage expanded significantly only in the 19th and 20th centuries.

This increasing state involvement has created a troubling contradiction: marriage is simultaneously treated as a sacred religious institution, a civil right, and a legal status with significant economic implications. The state's definition of marriage has continuously evolved—from prohibitions on interracial marriage to the recognition of same-sex marriage—demonstrating that government-defined marriage is not a fixed institution but rather a constantly shifting legal construct reflecting the values of those in power.

The Equality Argument

State-recognized marriage inherently privileges certain relationships over others. It creates a two-tiered system of relationships—those deemed worthy of legal recognition and benefits, and those that are not. This system discriminates against individuals who choose not to marry, cannot legally marry under current laws, or whose relationships do not fit traditional models.

Consider the unmarried cohabitating couple who care deeply for each other but choose not to marry; the group of friends who live together for decades providing mutual support; or the extended family members who function as primary caregivers to one another. These relationships receive none of the legal protections or economic benefits afforded to married couples, despite potentially featuring the same commitment, care, and interdependence.

By removing marriage from the state's purview, we would eliminate this hierarchy of relationships. No longer would the government decide which personal bonds deserve recognition and which do not. This would represent true equality under the law, where individuals—not the state—determine the significance and structure of their intimate relationships.

Religious Freedom and Separation of Church and State

Marriage holds profound religious significance for many people, yet civil marriage laws inevitably conflict with some religious conceptions of marriage. This creates an untenable situation where the state is effectively defining an institution that many consider sacred, potentially violating the principle of separation of church and state.

By privatizing marriage, we would fully separate religious marriage from civil law. Religious institutions would remain free to define marriage according to their own beliefs and traditions, without state interference. Conversely, the state would no longer impose any particular conception of marriage—religious or secular—on society as a whole. This clean separation would protect religious freedom while preventing religious definitions from being imposed on those who do not share those beliefs.

Individual Liberty and Personal Autonomy

Perhaps the strongest argument for abolishing state marriage is its advancement of individual liberty. In a free society, shouldn't adults have the right to define their own relationships without government approval or involvement? The current system dictates not only who can marry but also how their relationship must be structured—a one-size-fits-all approach that fails to accommodate the rich diversity of human relationships.

Privatizing marriage would allow individuals to create relationship agreements tailored to their specific needs, values, and circumstances. Those desiring religious marriages could pursue those through their faith communities. Others might create detailed contracts establishing rights and responsibilities between partners. Some might forgo formal recognition entirely, allowing relationships to exist on their own terms.

This approach recognizes that intimate relationships are deeply personal matters that should be governed by individual choice rather than state mandate. It returns decision-making power to where it belongs—with the people directly involved in the relationship.

Economic and Administrative Efficiency

The current marriage system creates countless economic distortions through tax benefits, penalties, inheritance laws, and other financial incentives and disincentives. These policies often lack coherent justification and frequently lead to arbitrary outcomes. For instance, the "marriage penalty" in taxation can result in married couples paying more taxes than they would as unmarried individuals, while others receive a "marriage bonus."

Abolishing state marriage would eliminate these distortions, allowing for a simpler, more neutral tax code and benefit system. Rather than using marital status as a proxy for economic interdependence or need, policies could be designed around more relevant factors like household size, actual economic relationships, or dependency.

Administrative efficiency would also improve as government agencies would no longer need to verify, record, and track marital status for countless purposes. The resources currently devoted to administering marriage licenses, processing divorces, and litigating marriage-related disputes could be redirected to more productive uses.

The Private Contract Alternative

What would replace state marriage? A system of private contracts and agreements, combined with generally applicable laws protecting vulnerable individuals regardless of relationship status.

Under this system, individuals would be free to create contracts establishing whatever rights, responsibilities, and commitments they desire in their relationships. These might include:

  • Property agreements defining ownership during the relationship and upon dissolution
  • Healthcare decision-making authorizations
  • Inheritance arrangements
  • Co-parenting agreements
  • Financial support commitments
  • Conflict resolution processes

For those who prefer simplicity, standard contract templates could be widely available. Religious institutions could continue to offer marriage ceremonies with whatever spiritual significance and community recognition they choose, separate from legal status.

This approach offers far greater flexibility than the current one-size-fits-all marriage model. It allows for personalization based on the unique needs and values of each relationship, rather than forcing conformity to a state-defined standard.

Addressing Common Concerns

Critics of privatizing marriage often raise legitimate concerns that deserve serious consideration:

What about children's interests? Children's wellbeing can and should be protected through laws that apply regardless of parents' marital status. Parental rights and responsibilities should be based on biological relationship or formal adoption, not marital status. Child support obligations should exist independent of any relationship between the parents.

What about vulnerable spouses? Current marriage laws do provide some protections for economically vulnerable spouses. However, these protections could be maintained through more targeted policies that apply based on actual economic dependence rather than marital status. Wouldn't this create legal chaos? A transition period would be necessary, but the legal system already handles complex relationship contracts in many contexts. Clear default rules could be established for existing marriages, and a gradual phase-in would allow for adjustment. The long-term benefits of a more flexible, fair system outweigh the temporary transition challenges.

Conclusion

The abolition of state-recognized marriage represents not a devaluation of committed relationships, but rather their liberation from government control. By removing marriage from the legal sphere and treating it as a private relationship or contract, we would enhance individual liberty, promote true equality under the law, respect religious freedom, increase economic efficiency, and better accommodate the diverse reality of modern relationships.

This reform would return marriage to its historical roots as a private commitment between individuals, recognized by their communities according to their own values and traditions—not by government license. It would allow each person to pursue relationships on their own terms, free from state dictates about what constitutes a valid partnership.

The time has come to end the state's role in marriage. By doing so, we would strengthen both personal freedom and relationship equality, creating a society where intimate bonds are defined by those who form them, not by the government that regulates them.

The Case for Abolishing State Marriage: Restoring Liberty, Equality, and Contractual Freedom

The state’s recognition and regulation of marriage is an anachronistic, coercive, and unjust institution that should be completely abolished. Government has no legitimate role in defining, licensing, subsidizing, or dissolving what is fundamentally a private interpersonal relationship or voluntary contract. The time has come to remove marriage entirely from the legal sphere, treating it as a purely private matter between consenting adults, much like friendship, religious vows, or any other significant personal commitment. This reform would enhance individual liberty, eliminate arbitrary discrimination, reduce government power, simplify the legal system, and allow diverse communities to define their own relationships according to conscience rather than bureaucratic fiat.

The Historical and Philosophical Illegitimacy of State Marriage

Marriage as a legal status is a relatively modern invention in its current form. For most of human history, marriage was regulated primarily by religious communities, kinship networks, and custom. The state’s heavy-handed involvement—through licensing, tax codes, inheritance laws, and family courts—is largely a product of 19th- and 20th-century centralization. This development represented a significant expansion of state power into the most intimate realm of human life. By granting the state the authority to decide who may marry whom, what constitutes a valid marriage, and what benefits attach to it, we have effectively allowed government to define a fundamental aspect of human identity and association.

This violates core liberal principles. John Stuart Mill’s harm principle is clear: the state should only interfere with individual liberty to prevent harm to others. Consensual adult relationships, whether romantic, sexual, economic, or platonic, do not inherently harm third parties. The state’s current marriage regime, by contrast, actively harms people by imposing a one-size-fits-all model backed by coercive power. It privileges certain relationship structures (typically monogamous, heterosexual, state-approved dyads) while denying equal treatment to others. Even after same-sex marriage was legalized in many jurisdictions, the system remains discriminatory: it excludes polyamorous groups, close friends who wish to share legal protections, elderly companions, and asexual or non-romantic partnerships that provide mutual care and support.

The Discriminatory Nature of State-Sanctioned Marriage

Marriage law is inherently exclusionary. No matter where the boundary is drawn, someone is left out. If marriage requires two people, it excludes polyamorous families who form stable, committed multi-partner households. If it requires sexual consummation or romantic love (as some older legal doctrines implied), it excludes companions, caregivers, and platonic partners who wish to gain hospital visitation rights, inheritance, or tax benefits. If it requires state licensing, it burdens those who reject government authority on religious or philosophical grounds.

By tying important legal rights—tax treatment, immigration, inheritance, medical decision-making, property division, and more—to a single state-defined status, we create a two-tiered system of citizenship. Those who conform to the government’s preferred relationship template receive a bundle of valuable privileges; everyone else must either forgo those rights or engage in complex, expensive legal workarounds such as trusts, powers of attorney, and cohabitation agreements.

This is both inefficient and unjust. It would be far simpler and more equitable to detach these rights from relationship status entirely and make them available on an individual or contractual basis. Hospital visitation, for example, should be a matter of patient designation, not marital status. Immigration sponsorship could be reformed to focus on genuine commitments attested by affidavits and evidence rather than a marriage certificate. Inheritance and property rights can be handled through private contracts, wills, and trusts without reference to marital status. The state’s current approach of bundling dozens of unrelated rights into a single “marriage” package is lazy governance that creates more problems than it solves.

Marriage as Contract, Not Status

The fundamental error lies in treating marriage as a status conferred by the state rather than a contract created by the parties themselves. In a free society, adults should be able to define their own commitments through private agreements. Want a monogamous lifelong religious covenant? Draft one with your partner and have it notarized or witnessed according to your faith. Want a renewable five-year renewable partnership with specific financial terms? Write it down. Want a platonic cohabitation and caregiving agreement with three adults? That should be permissible as well, provided all parties are consenting adults.

Critics often claim this would create chaos or uncertainty. Yet commercial contracts routinely handle far more complex arrangements—partnerships, corporations, LLCs, joint ventures—without requiring state approval of the underlying relationship. Real estate, business, and employment relationships generate vastly more economic value and potential for dispute than most marriages, yet we allow private ordering with minimal state interference beyond basic contract enforcement. There is no principled reason why domestic relationships should be treated differently.

Private marriage contracts could specify property division, support obligations, inheritance, dispute resolution (including choice of religious or secular arbitration), and grounds for termination. Standard templates would emerge, just as they have for prenuptial agreements today. Courts would enforce them under ordinary contract law, with the same rules against fraud, duress, and unconscionability that govern other agreements. This system would be more transparent, more tailored to individual needs, and less prone to the arbitrary whims of family court judges.

The Benefits of Abolition

Complete abolition of state marriage would yield multiple benefits:

Liberty. Individuals would be free to structure their most intimate relationships without seeking permission from the state. No more marriage licenses. No more waiting periods. No more government officials deciding whose love is legitimate.

Equality. Rather than constantly expanding or contracting the definition of marriage through political battles, we would eliminate the privileged status altogether. All relationships would stand or fall on their own merits and the contracts parties choose to make.

Simplicity and Efficiency. The legal system would be vastly simplified. Instead of complex marital property regimes, community property rules, and alimony statutes that vary by jurisdiction, parties would rely on clear, voluntarily chosen contracts. Divorce proceedings would be replaced by contract enforcement actions.

Reduced Government Power. The state would lose a powerful tool for social engineering. Historically, marriage law has been used to enforce racial, gender, and religious norms. Even today it serves as a vehicle for redistributing wealth according to political preferences. Removing this power from government is inherently desirable for anyone who values limited government.

Religious Freedom. Churches, temples, and other religious bodies could define marriage according to their own doctrines without worrying about whether the state will recognize their ceremonies. A Catholic couple could have a sacramental marriage that differs from a Muslim nikah or a secular commitment ceremony. The Case for Complete Privatization of Marriage

Removing the State from the Altar

The institution of marriage has existed for millennia, predating modern governments, legal systems, and even organized religion as we know it today. Yet somewhere along the historical path, the state inserted itself into what was fundamentally a private arrangement between individuals, families, and communities. This intervention, however well-intentioned, has created a legal morass that violates principles of individual liberty, religious freedom, and equal treatment under the law. The time has come to recognize that marriage should be entirely removed from the legal sphere and returned to its rightful place as a private relationship or contract between consenting adults.

The Historical Accident of State Marriage

The state's involvement in marriage was never inevitable or philosophically necessary. For most of human history, marriages were matters of religious ceremony, family arrangement, or simple mutual agreement between partners. Government licensing of marriage emerged relatively recently, often for purposes we would now find repugnant—controlling inheritance among nobility, preventing interracial unions, or regulating the poor. The marriage license, in many jurisdictions, originated as a tool of exclusion rather than inclusion.

Today, we have inherited this system without questioning its fundamental premises. We assume that because the state regulates marriage, it must regulate marriage. This is the fallacy of tradition masquerading as necessity. The state also once regulated who could enter which professions based on guild membership, which books could be printed, and which religions could be practiced. We abandoned those intrusions on liberty. Marriage regulation should follow.

The Liberty Argument

At its core, the case for marriage privatization rests on the principle that individuals should be free to structure their intimate relationships as they see fit, without requiring government approval. When two or more adults wish to commit to one another, to share their lives, resources, and futures, what legitimate interest does the state have in approving or denying that arrangement?

The current system requires citizens to petition their government for permission to marry. They must meet criteria established by legislators, obtain licenses, and have their unions certified by state-approved officiants. This framework treats marriage as a privilege granted by the state rather than a right exercised by free individuals. Such a conception is fundamentally incompatible with a society that values personal autonomy and limited government.

Consider the absurdity from another angle: the state does not require licenses for friendship, for business partnerships among intimates, or for religious fellowship. Why should it require one for the particular form of committed relationship we call marriage? The state's involvement implies that marriage is somehow the government's business, that it has ownership over the institution. It does not.

The Religious Freedom Argument

The entanglement of civil and religious marriage creates perpetual conflict in a pluralistic society. Different religious traditions hold vastly different views on what constitutes a valid marriage. Some recognize only unions between one man and one woman. Others bless same-sex unions. Some traditions permit polygamous arrangements. Others have specific requirements about interfaith marriage, previous divorces, or ceremonial necessities.

When the state defines marriage, it inevitably privileges some religious conceptions over others. This creates the impossible task of crafting a legal definition that respects all faiths while satisfying none completely. Religious communities find themselves either fighting to impose their definition on civil law or fighting against definitions they find spiritually invalid being imposed upon their members.

Privatization elegantly resolves this conflict. Without state-defined marriage, each religious community would be free to recognize whichever unions comport with their theology. A Catholic church could maintain its traditional standards without any implication that the state endorses those standards. A progressive congregation could bless unions the Catholic church would not, without any implication that they are forcing the Catholic church to do likewise. The culture wars over marriage would lose their legal battlefield because there would be nothing legal to fight over.

The Equality Argument

Paradoxically, removing marriage from the law entirely may better serve equality than continuing to expand the legal definition of marriage. Throughout history, marginalized groups have had to petition and fight for inclusion in the institution of civil marriage. Interracial couples fought this battle. Same-sex couples fought it more recently. Polyamorous individuals continue to face exclusion.

Each expansion of marriage rights requires immense political effort, legal battles, and social upheaval. And after each expansion, a new boundary exists, with new people on the outside. The pattern will continue indefinitely as long as the state maintains any definition of marriage at all, because any definition necessarily includes and excludes.

True equality in intimate relationships cannot be achieved through endless expansion of a state institution. It can only be achieved by removing the state from the equation entirely. When marriage is a private matter, no one requires government validation of their relationship. No one is told their love is legally inferior. No one must win a political campaign to have their commitment recognized.

The Practical Mechanisms

Critics of marriage privatization often ask, "But what about all the legal benefits attached to marriage?" This question, while understandable, reveals a failure of imagination. Every practical function currently served by legal marriage can be accomplished through private contracts and targeted legislation that makes no reference to marital status.

Property and finances: Partners can create contracts governing shared property, joint accounts, and financial obligations. This already happens with prenuptial and postnuptial agreements. Without state marriage, such contracts would become standard practice, likely with template forms as accessible as current marriage licenses.

Medical decisions and hospital visitation: These can be governed by healthcare proxies and powers of attorney—documents that are already necessary for unmarried partners and often advisable even for married couples. Legislation can ensure that individuals may designate any person they choose for such purposes.

Inheritance: Wills and trusts already govern inheritance for those who use them. The state could adopt default inheritance rules based on designated beneficiaries or cohabitation rather than marriage.

Immigration: This represents one of the trickier areas, but solutions exist. Immigration policy could focus on genuine relationships of interdependence, evaluated individually, rather than relying on the proxy of marriage. This would actually be more effective at identifying fraudulent arrangements than the current system.

Parental rights: These should be governed by parentage law entirely separate from marriage. The current system already must address parental rights for unmarried parents, step-parents, and others outside the marital model. A robust parentage framework, independent of marriage, serves children better than assuming parental rights flow from marital status.

Taxation and benefits: The joint filing status and other marital tax benefits could be replaced with systems based on household composition or economic interdependence. Social Security survivor benefits could be reformed to allow designation of beneficiaries. Employer benefits could be offered to any designated household member.

Each of these reforms recognizes that what matters legally is the specific function—decision-making authority, property rights, care for dependents—not the romantic or religious status of "marriage" itself.

Answering Objections

"Marriage provides stability for children." Children benefit from stable households with committed caregivers. However, the legal status of marriage does not create that stability—the commitment of the adults does. Many married households are unstable; many unmarried households are paragons of stability. Moreover, marriage privatization does not prevent commitment; it merely removes government certification of that commitment. Private marriage contracts could include provisions regarding children, and parentage law would continue to protect children's interests.

"Society has an interest in promoting marriage." Society promotes many valuable things—education, health, community involvement—without requiring government licenses. If marriage is valuable, its value should be evident without state endorsement. And if it requires state endorsement to maintain its value, perhaps what we are preserving is not genuine value but mere legal privilege.

"Marriage privatization is politically impossible." Perhaps today. But so was marriage equality in 1990, interracial marriage in 1950, or women's suffrage in 1870. The arc of history bends toward liberty when advocates make the case persistently and persuasively. Moreover, marriage privatization may represent a rare point of convergence between libertarians who oppose state involvement in personal matters, progressives who see traditional marriage as a patriarchal institution, religious conservatives tired of fighting to protect their definition of marriage, and polyamorous communities who will otherwise remain perpetually excluded.

"Marriage is a foundational social institution." It is precisely because marriage is so important that we should not trust it to government management. The state is a blunt instrument, capable of licensing and regulating but not of nurturing the deep human needs that marriage addresses. Those needs are better served by families, communities, religious institutions, and the partners themselves. Privatization does not destroy marriage; it frees marriage from bureaucratic capture.

A Vision of Marriage Unbound

Imagine a world where marriage is what it always should have been: a profound commitment between partners, witnessed by those they love, structured according to their own values and needs. Some would marry in grand religious ceremonies. Others would exchange vows privately. Some would enter detailed legal contracts governing every aspect of their shared lives. Others would proceed on trust and love alone. Some would have monogamous marriages. Others, where all parties consent, might construct different arrangements.

In this world, no couple would wait anxiously for a legislature or court to validate their relationship. No religious community would fear government intrusion into its sacred definitions. No bureaucrat would stand between two people and their commitment to one another.

This is not a radical vision. It is, in many ways, a return to how humans organized their intimate lives for most of history, updated with modern legal tools that protect individual rights and settle disputes. It is a recognition that the government overstep of the past few centuries, however normalized, was never philosophically justified.

Conclusion

The case for removing marriage from the legal sphere is ultimately a case for human freedom and dignity. It recognizes that intimate relationships are too important to be defined by legislatures, too varied to be captured in statutory categories, and too sacred—in whatever sense individuals understand that word—to require bureaucratic blessing.

Marriage privatization would end the culture wars over marriage by removing the prize being fought over. It would protect religious freedom by ensuring no faith's definition is privileged or burdened by law. It would advance equality by eliminating the very legal distinctions that create unequal classes of relationships. And it would honor liberty by recognizing that free adults can structure their own lives without seeking permission from the state.

The state should protect individual rights, enforce contracts, and settle disputes. It should not be in the business of certifying love, sanctifying commitment, or defining family. Marriage belongs to the people who enter into it, not to the government that currently presumes to license it.

It is time to complete the separation of marriage and state.
